extracted.intended_audience: public company management, investor relations officers, corporate counsel, and PR/communications teams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance about complying with the U.S. SEC's Regulation FD (Fair Disclosure): what disclosures are prohibited, exceptions, acceptable dissemination venues (including social media), who is covered, and enforcement implications. Useful for preparing press releases, earnings calls, and other investor communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on selective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject to certain limited exceptions, the rules generally prohibit public companies from disclosing previously nonpublic, material information to certain parties unless the information is distributed to the public first or simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation sought to stamp out selective disclosure in which some investors received market-moving information before others; ensure material, nonpublic information is released broadly (public first or at the same time) rather than privately to selected analysts or institutional investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insider exception / confidentiality agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Selective disclosure may be made so long as the company first collects a confidentiality agreement from the other party (or the other party is already subject to a duty of trust and confidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The confidentiality agreement need not include an undertaking not to trade on the information. Paragraph (b) of Rule 100 states the rule does not apply to disclosures to persons bound by duties of trust or confidence (e.g., 'temporary' insiders like outside consultants — attorneys, investment bankers, accountants — and any person who has expressly agreed to maintain the information in confidence). Disclosure to insiders or temporary insiders is permitted because their misuse would subject them to insider trading liability (e.g., under Rule 10b-5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Venues and social media requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies can use social media to disseminate information if certain requirements are met: investors’ access to the chosen social media platform must not be restricted and investors must be notified about which social media will be used to disseminate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat approved social media like company websites: ensure broad, unrestricted investor access and give prior notice to investors about which platform(s) will be used. (SEC clarified this position on April 2, 2013.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality and public record scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule only prohibits private disclosure of material information. Companies may disclose public record information to analysts without necessarily violating the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of 'seemingly inconsequential data' that could be material in aggregation (mosaic theory). Evaluate whether information, even if small in isolation, could be material when combined with other public or private pieces of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability — covered recipients and permitted communications
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule applies to certain groups such as securities market professionals and shareholders, but allows companies to continue providing necessary information to business partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which recipient categories are covered by Reg FD (e.g., market professionals, shareholders) and which business communications remain permissible; tailor disclosures and confidentiality practices accordingly so necessary operational disclosures to partners are not inadvertently restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of Regulation FD can lead to SEC enforcement actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reg FD has been enforced intermittently (example: in 2017 the SEC charged TherapeuticsMD), so companies should treat compliance seriously when preparing press releases, conference calls, social media disclosures, and private communications to avoid enforcement risk.
